# Session 1 · Mon Nov 9 {.section}
## Why Distribute Data? Replication, Sharding, and Single Points of Failure

::: {.notes}
**Full-session timing plan (50 min total, ~15 min of which is Checkpoint 6 itself):**

| Slide | Time |
|---|---|
| Recap: From Compute to Storage | 3 min |
| The Problem: One Machine, Too Much Load | 4 min |
| Replication: Many Copies of the Same Data | 4 min |
| Sharding: Splitting the Data Itself | 4 min |
| Replication vs. Sharding — Choosing Between Them | 5 min |
| The Cost of Replication | 3 min |
| The Cost of Sharding | 3 min |
| Single Points of Failure, Revisited | 3 min |
| Checkpoint 6 | 15 min |
| Bridge to Wednesday | 2 min |

9 content slides (~31 min) + Checkpoint 6. This is Module 5's foundation session — Wednesday
builds directly on today's replication/sharding vocabulary by asking "and what does CAP have to
say about it?"
:::

---

## Recap: From Compute to Storage

Module 4 answered "how do you *compute* something at scale?" — load data into Spark, transform
it, aggregate it, write out a result.

Module 5 answers the next question: **where does that result actually live**, once it's
computed, so that thousands of users can read it reliably at the same time? A single machine
running a single database has exactly the same limits Module 3 opened with — one disk, one CPU,
one point of failure — just for *storage* instead of *processing*.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Quick bridge only — the point is that "why distribute" is a question we've
already answered once (Module 3's big-data motivation), now being asked again about storage
specifically.
:::

---

## The Problem: One Machine, Too Much Load

A single database server can fail in two different ways as demand grows, and they call for two
different fixes:

- **Too much traffic, data fits fine:** the machine simply can't answer requests fast enough —
  every read and write funnels through one CPU, one network connection.
- **Too much data, traffic is fine:** the dataset itself no longer fits on one machine's disk (or
  even in a reasonable multiple of it), regardless of how much traffic there is.
- **Single point of failure**, either way: if that one machine goes down, the data is completely
  unreachable until it comes back — recall Module 2's "partial failures" idea, except now there's
  nothing partial about it. One machine down means *everything* is down.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Setting up the two-problems framing explicitly here pays off on the very next
two slides — replication answers the first bullet, sharding answers the second.
:::

---

## Replication: Many Copies of the Same Data

**Replication** means keeping multiple full copies of the same data on different machines.

- Every replica holds the **entire** dataset — not a piece of it.
- Reads can be served by **any** replica, spreading read traffic across multiple machines instead
  of funneling it through one.
- If one replica goes down, the others still have every record — the single-point-of-failure
  problem from the last slide goes away for reads.
- Writes are more subtle: usually one replica (the **primary**) accepts writes, and the change is
  then copied out to the others.

::: {.callout-important}
You've actually seen a first, simpler version of this already: Module 3's HDFS stored each block
on 3 machines — like stocking the same ingredient at 3 kitchen branches, so one branch's fridge
breaking down doesn't lose it. That was replication for *file blocks*, specifically for MapReduce
jobs to read. Today's version is the general idea, for *any* database, read and written directly
by users — not just batch jobs.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)
One database-cylinder icon labeled "Primary" at the top, with two arrows fanning down to two more
cylinder icons labeled "Replica 1" and "Replica 2," each holding an identical small stack of
document icons (same three icons repeated in all three cylinders, to show it's a *full* copy each
time). A read arrow pointing into any of the three; a write arrow pointing only into the Primary.
Caption: "Same data, three times over. Reads go anywhere. Writes go through the primary."
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Keep the "primary accepts writes" detail brief here — Session 2 goes deep on
exactly *how* that copying happens (sync vs. async) and why it matters for consistency.
:::

---

## Sharding: Splitting the Data Itself

**Sharding** means splitting the dataset itself across multiple machines — each machine holds a
different **slice** of the data, not a full copy.

```
Shard key: user_id

Shard 1: user_id 0 – 9,999,999
Shard 2: user_id 10,000,000 – 19,999,999
Shard 3: user_id 20,000,000+
```

- Each shard holds only **its own fraction** of the total data — together, all shards make up the
  whole dataset.
- Both **storage** and **write traffic** get spread across machines, since different records live
  (and are written) on different shards.
- The field used to decide which shard a record belongs to is called the **shard key**.
- A query for one specific record only needs to go to the one shard that holds it — but a query
  that spans many records may need to check every shard.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Contrast explicitly with the previous slide's diagram: replication = same data
N times; sharding = 1/N of the data, N times. That contrast is the single most important idea in
today's session.
:::

---

## Replication vs. Sharding — Choosing Between Them

| | Replication | Sharding |
|---|---|---|
| **Solves** | Read throughput, availability | Data volume, write throughput |
| **Each node holds** | A full copy of all the data | A fraction of the data |
| **Use when** | The dataset fits on one machine, but there's too much read traffic | The dataset itself is too large for one machine |
| **Single point of failure?** | Fixed — any replica can serve reads if another fails | Not fixed by sharding alone — losing one shard still loses *its* slice of data |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
A photo-sharing app's user-profile database is only 2 GB (tiny), but gets 200,000 profile-page
views per second during a viral event. A separate table logging every photo upload has grown to
40 TB and keeps growing. Which table needs replication, which needs sharding, and could a table
ever need **both**?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** The callout's last question is the important one to land: yes, a table can
need both at once (e.g., MongoDB's sharded clusters replicate *within* each shard) — that's
exactly what Session 5's "Replication and Sharding in MongoDB" slides come back to.
:::

---

## The Cost of Replication

Replication isn't free — it trades storage and consistency for read throughput and availability.

- **Storage cost multiplies:** 3 replicas means 3× the storage for the same data.
- **Replicas can briefly disagree:** if a write hasn't finished copying to every replica yet, a
  read from a lagging replica can return **stale** (out-of-date) data.
- This lag is usually milliseconds, but it is never exactly zero — "how much staleness is
  acceptable" is a real design decision, not a solved problem. Session 2 goes deep on this.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Plant this seed deliberately — "replicas can briefly disagree" is precisely
what Wednesday's session expands into strong vs. eventual consistency.
:::

---

## The Cost of Sharding

Sharding isn't free either — it trades query simplicity for scale.

- **Cross-shard queries are expensive:** "find everyone named Alice" now has to ask *every* shard
  and merge the results, instead of asking one machine.
- **A bad shard key creates hot spots:** if your shard key clusters too much traffic onto one
  shard (e.g., sharding by signup date when everyone signs up "today"), that one shard becomes the
  new single overloaded machine — sharding stops helping.
- **Resharding is hard:** once data is split across shards, changing the shard key later means
  physically moving large amounts of data between machines.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** The hot-spot point is the one worth emphasizing if time is short — it's the
most common real mistake, and it directly explains *why* choosing a good shard key matters, not
just that one is required.
:::

---

## Single Points of Failure, Revisited

Tie this back to Module 2: a **single point of failure (SPOF)** is any one component whose
failure takes down the whole system. An un-replicated database is a textbook SPOF.

- Replication removes the SPOF **for reads** — any surviving replica can still answer queries.
- It does **not**, by itself, remove the SPOF for writes if there's still exactly one primary
  accepting them — if the primary goes down, *something* has to take over, which is a real,
  nontrivial problem (this is exactly the mechanism behind the GitHub split-brain case study from
  Module 2, Session 3 — a failover mechanism promoting a new primary is precisely what created
  that incident).
- Sharding, on its own, does not remove any SPOF — it just changes *what* is lost when one machine
  fails: instead of losing everything, you lose that shard's slice of the data.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Explicitly naming the GitHub case study connection here rewards students who
retained Module 2 — say it out loud rather than assuming they'll make the connection themselves.
:::

---

## The CAP Theorem, Revisited for Storage

::: {.notes}
**Full-session timing plan (50 min total):**

| Slide | Time |

| Recap: The CAP Theorem (from Module 2) | 3 min |

| Strong Consistency | 4 min |

| Read Preference: Choosing Where to Read From | 4 min |
| Consistency Is a Spectrum, Not a Switch | 4 min |
| Bridge to Friday's Worksheet | 3 min |

10 slides, ~40 min. This session leans on Module 2's CAP content directly — don't re-derive the
theorem from scratch, just re-anchor it and apply it.
:::

---

## Recap: Replication's Loose Thread

Monday ended on an unresolved tension: replicas are supposed to hold "the same data," but a write
takes time to copy from the primary to every replica. **For that window of time, they don't quite
agree.**

Today's question: what should a read do when it lands in that window?

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** This is the whole session in one sentence — keep this slide tight so it lands
as a genuine open question, not a rhetorical one.
:::

---

## Recap: The CAP Theorem (from Module 2)

Module 2, Session 2 covered this in full — a fast re-anchor:

| | |
|---|---|
| **C**onsistency | Every read gets the latest write, or an error |
| **A**vailability | Every request gets *a* response |
| **P**artition tolerance | The system keeps working despite a network split |

**The theorem:** during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between
Consistency and Availability — it cannot fully guarantee both at once.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Genuinely just a recap slide — if a student is shaky on this, point them back
to Module 2's slides rather than re-teaching the proof sketch here.
:::

---

## Applying CAP to a Replicated Database

A replica set (Monday's picture: one primary, several replicas) is itself a small distributed
system — so CAP applies to it directly.

- If a **network partition** separates a replica from the primary, that replica has a choice:
  - **Refuse to answer reads** until it can confirm it's caught up (favors **Consistency**)
  - **Answer with whatever data it currently has**, possibly stale (favors **Availability**)
- This is *exactly* Module 2's CAP trade-off, just applied to "should this specific replica answer
  this specific read" instead of "should the whole system answer this specific request."

::: {.callout-important}
Even **without** a network partition, replication introduces a smaller version of this same
choice: does the primary wait for replicas to confirm a write before telling the client "done" —
trading speed for certainty — or does it say "done" immediately and let the copying happen in the
background? That's the next four slides.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** The callout is the pivot from "CAP during rare partitions" to "consistency
trade-offs during totally normal operation" — make sure that shift is explicit, since it's easy
to think CAP only matters when something is broken.
:::

---

## Strong Consistency

**Strong consistency:** every read reflects the most recent write, no matter which
replica answers it.

- To guarantee this, a write typically can't be considered "done" until it has been confirmed by
  enough replicas that no read could possibly see stale data.
- **Cost:** writes are slower — the primary has to wait for confirmation before responding to the
  client.
- **Benefit:** no surprises. Once a write succeeds, every subsequent read, from any replica, sees
  it.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Keep this and the next slide symmetric in structure (definition → cost →
benefit) so the contrast is easy to hold in mind together.
:::

---

## Eventual Consistency

**Eventual consistency:** replicas are allowed to be temporarily out of sync — but if no new
writes happen, they will all *eventually* converge to the same value.

- The primary can respond "done" to the client as soon as **it** has the write, without waiting
  for replicas to catch up.
- **Cost:** a read immediately after a write might hit a replica that hasn't caught up yet, and
  see the old value.
- **Benefit:** writes are fast, and the system keeps working even if a replica is temporarily
  slow or unreachable.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
Quiz 7 will ask about this directly: **asynchronous replication can lead to replicas temporarily
having different versions of the data.** Why "asynchronous," specifically — what would
*synchronous* replication have to do differently to prevent that?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** The callout's answer is the bridge into the next slide: synchronous replication
would have to wait for replicas to confirm before acknowledging the write — which is strong
consistency's mechanism, described from the replication-mechanics angle instead of the CAP angle.
:::

---

## Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Replication

This is the actual mechanism behind the strong/eventual distinction:

| | Synchronous replication | Asynchronous replication |
|---|---|---|
| Primary waits for replicas before confirming write? | Yes | No |
| Write speed | Slower | Faster |
| Consistency | Strong | Eventual |
| Risk if primary crashes right after a write | None — replicas already have it | Replicas may be missing the most recent write(s) |

- **Synchronous** = strong consistency's mechanism: the primary refuses to say "done" until
  replicas confirm.
- **Asynchronous** = eventual consistency's mechanism: the primary says "done" immediately and
  copies the change out afterward.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** This table is the payoff of the whole strong-vs-eventual discussion — make
sure students leave able to map "strong consistency" → "synchronous replication" and "eventual
consistency" → "asynchronous replication" without hesitation.
:::

---

## A Worked Scenario: Checking Your Bank Balance

You just transferred $500 out of your checking account. One second later, you refresh the app and
check your balance.

- **If the bank uses strong consistency:** your new balance is guaranteed correct, every time —
  worth the extra write latency for money, where "slightly out of date" is unacceptable.
- **If the bank instead used eventual consistency and you got unlucky:** you might briefly see
  your *old* balance, as if the transfer hadn't happened — even though it genuinely went through.
- Compare this to a **social media "like" count**: if that count is briefly off by one because of
  replication lag, essentially nobody notices or cares.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
Name one more real system where you'd insist on strong consistency, and one more where eventual
consistency would be perfectly fine. What's the actual property that decides which one you pick?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** The intended takeaway for the callout: the deciding property is roughly "cost
of showing stale data" versus "cost of slower writes" — not some fixed rule about what kind of app
it is.
:::

---

## Read Preference: Choosing Where to Read From

Many real databases let you choose, **per query**, how strict to be — rather than picking strong
or eventual consistency for the whole system once and for all.

- **Read from the primary:** always current, but funnels all reads through one machine — no
  read-scaling benefit from having replicas at all.
- **Read from any replica** ("secondary" reads): spreads read load across machines, at the cost of
  possibly-stale results.
- This setting is usually called **read preference**, and it's a real, named option you'll see
  again in MongoDB specifically, in Session 5.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Flag explicitly that this is forward-referencing real MongoDB terminology —
students will see "read preference" again in two sessions and should recognize it as the same idea
introduced here, not a new concept.
:::

---

## Consistency Is a Spectrum, Not a Switch

Strong and eventual consistency are the two ends of a range, not the only two options:

- Some systems let you require confirmation from just **some** replicas (not all, not just one) —
  a middle ground between the two extremes.
- Some systems guarantee **causal consistency**: if event B happened *because of* event A, every
  node sees A before B — even if unrelated events can still arrive in different orders on
  different nodes.
- The exact terminology varies by database. What matters for this course: consistency is a design
  **choice with a dial**, not a single fixed property a database either has or doesn't.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Keep this conceptual and brief — the goal is "there's more nuance here than
strong-vs-eventual if you go looking," not to teach every consistency model by name.
:::

---

## In-Class Activity: The Storage Design Worksheet

::: {.notes}

| Slide | Time |

**Instructor note:** work scenarios in groups of 2–3, on paper or a shared doc. For each, groups
should decide: replicate, shard, both, or neither — and if replicating, strong or eventual
consistency, and why. There is genuine room for disagreement on all three; resist giving "the"
right answer during group work, save it for the discussion slide.
:::

---

## Framing: No New Concepts Today

Everything you need is already covered: replication, sharding, single points of failure (Monday);
strong vs. eventual consistency, synchronous vs. asynchronous replication (Wednesday).

Today's job: **combine** those tools into an actual design decision, for three different
scenarios, and defend your reasoning to the class.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 2 min.** Set expectations: this is discussion and small-group work, not a lecture.
:::

---

## Scenario 1: A Note-Taking App

A note-taking app has 3 million users. Each user's notes are small (a few KB total) and are read
and written almost exclusively by that one user — nobody else ever sees your notes.

**In your group, decide:** replicate, shard, both, or neither? If replicating, strong or eventual
consistency? What's the worst thing that happens if you get this wrong?

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 10 min including group work.** Push toward: total data volume is enormous (3M users ×
notes) but each *individual* user's working set is tiny and only touched by one person — this
maps cleanly to sharding by user ID, with mild replication for availability; strong consistency
isn't very important since each user only ever reads their own writes.
:::

---

## Scenario 2: A Flight-Search Engine

A flight-search engine stores current seat availability for every flight, globally. Millions of
users search and book simultaneously. Double-booking the same seat is a serious, costly problem.

**In your group, decide:** replicate, shard, both, or neither? If replicating, strong or eventual
consistency? What's the worst thing that happens if you get this wrong?

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 10 min including group work.** Push toward: this is the strong-consistency case — two
people should never be told the same seat is available after one of them already booked it. Sharding
by flight/route is reasonable for scale, but each shard's availability data needs strong
consistency, not eventual.
:::

---

## Scenario 3: A Multiplayer Game's Leaderboard

A multiplayer game shows a global "Top 100 players this week" leaderboard, updated as players
finish matches. Millions of matches finish per hour, worldwide.

**In your group, decide:** replicate, shard, both, or neither? If replicating, strong or eventual
consistency? What's the worst thing that happens if you get this wrong?

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 10 min including group work.** Push toward: extremely high write volume (matches
finishing constantly) argues for sharding; the leaderboard itself tolerates real staleness — if
your new high score takes a few seconds to appear, nobody is harmed — so eventual consistency is
an easy, correct call here, in sharp contrast to Scenario 2.
:::

---

## Class Discussion: Comparing Answers

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it — full class, 10–12 min
Compare your group's Scenario 2 (flight seats) and Scenario 3 (leaderboard) answers side by side.
Both have huge write volume. Why did one need strong consistency and the other didn't? What's the
*actual* question you should ask yourself to decide, for any new system?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 12 min.** Push toward: the deciding question isn't "how much traffic" — it's "what's
the cost of a user briefly seeing wrong/stale data, versus the cost of slower writes." Scale
determines *whether you need to shard*; the cost of staleness determines *how consistent you need
to be*. These are two separate axes, and today's scenarios were picked to make that separation
visible.
:::

---

## Wrap-Up

Every real storage decision in this course — and in industry — comes down to combining the same
handful of tools you now have: replicate for availability and read scale, shard for volume and
write scale, and dial consistency to match how much staleness a given piece of data can tolerate.

**Monday: what kind of database actually implements these tools — the landscape of NoSQL database
types.**

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 6 min** (including whatever discussion time is left over from the previous slide).
Close on the forward-reference to keep momentum into Monday.
:::

## Recap: Storage Design Is Solved — Now, What Software?

The last three sessions covered *concepts* that apply to any storage system — replication,
sharding, consistency. Today: the actual **kinds of database software** that implement these
concepts, and which kind fits which job.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Fast bridge — the shift is from "storage design theory" to "here are the
products."
:::

---

## Why Not Just a Relational Database?

Relational databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) are excellent for structured, transactional data — and
remain the right choice for a huge share of real applications. They start to struggle when you
need to:

- Store data whose structure **varies** from record to record (not every record has the same
  fields)
- **Scale out**, in Module 3's terms — spread both data and load across many machines — rather
  than **scale up** (buying one increasingly expensive bigger machine)
- Serve extremely high read or write volume with a simpler, less rigid query model

**NoSQL** ("Not only SQL") databases are a family of alternatives designed around these needs.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Resist framing this as "NoSQL is better" — it's a trade-off, and the slide
right before the module summary makes that explicit again.
:::

---

## The NoSQL Landscape

| Type | Data Model | Examples | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Document** | JSON-like documents | MongoDB, CouchDB | User profiles, product catalogs, flexible records |
| **Key-Value** | Plain key → value | Redis, DynamoDB | Caching, sessions, extremely simple lookups |
| **Column-Family** | Rows with dynamic columns, optimized for huge write volume | Cassandra, HBase | Time-series, write-heavy logging |
| **Graph** | Nodes and edges with relationships | Neo4j | Social networks, recommendations, fraud detection |

We focus on **document stores** (MongoDB) for the rest of this module — the most common
general-purpose choice in industry, and what the capstone uses.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 7 Q4 tests "which type is MongoDB" directly — make sure "document store"
sticks as MongoDB's category before moving on.
:::

---

## Document Stores — The Mental Model

- Data is stored as **documents** — JSON-like objects — instead of rows in a table.
- Documents in the same collection **do not need identical fields.**
- There's no schema to define upfront — you just insert documents, and the structure can vary.

```json
// User document
{ "name": "Alice", "email": "alice@example.com", "premium": true }

// Another user document — different fields, same collection
{ "name": "Bob", "email": "bob@example.com", "age": 29, "plan": "free" }
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Flexible schema is a genuine trade-off, not a pure win: nothing stops one document from having a
typo'd field name that silently doesn't match the others — the database won't catch it for you.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 7 Q7 tests this exact property (two documents, same collection, different
fields — true). The callout previews the "cost" side that the module-end trade-off slide expands
on.
:::

---

## Key-Value Stores

The simplest possible model: every value is stored under a unique key, and that's it.

```
SET session:abc123 "user_id=42,expires=..."
GET session:abc123
```

- The database treats the value as an **opaque blob** — it doesn't know or care what's inside.
- Extremely fast, often **in-memory** (Redis) — ideal when you always look things up by one exact
  key and don't need to query by the value's contents.
- Common uses: caching, session storage, rate limiting, real-time leaderboards.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Tie "real-time leaderboards" back to Session 3's Scenario 3 — same use case,
now with a concrete technology attached to it.
:::

---

## Column-Family Stores

Designed for **massive write throughput** distributed across many machines — think logging
billions of events per day.

- Rows have a partition key; the set of columns can vary per row within a partition (similar
  flexibility idea to document stores, different underlying structure).
- No joins, and query patterns are deliberately limited — you design your tables around the
  specific queries you'll run, not the other way around.
- Used by companies with enormous, constant write volume: Netflix, Apple, Instagram all use
  Cassandra for parts of their infrastructure.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Keep this brief relative to document/key-value — it's the least directly
relevant type to this course's labs and capstone, included for landscape completeness and because
Quiz 7 references NoSQL types generally.
:::

---

## Graph Databases

Built around **relationships** as first-class data, not an afterthought.

- **Nodes** (entities) and **edges** (relationships between them), both of which can have their
  own properties.
- Query language example (Neo4j's Cypher): `MATCH (a:Person)-[:FRIEND]->(b:Person) RETURN b`
- Ideal when the interesting questions are about *connections*: "friends of friends," "people who
  bought A also bought B," fraud rings, recommendation engines.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 7 Q5's recommendation-engine question maps directly here — say the
"people who bought A also bought B" phrase out loud, since it's close to the quiz's own wording.
:::

---

## Choosing the Right Type

| Scenario | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Flexible, general-purpose records — user profiles, catalogs | Document (MongoDB) |
| Exact-key lookups, need extreme speed | Key-value (Redis) |
| Enormous, constant write volume | Column-family (Cassandra) |
| The interesting question is about relationships | Graph (Neo4j) |
| Transactions, strict schema, strong consistency by default | Relational (PostgreSQL/MySQL) |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
A ride-sharing app needs: (1) driver profile records that vary a bit driver-to-driver, (2) a
constant firehose of GPS location pings from every active driver, and (3) "which drivers are
friends/referred each other" for a referral bonus program. Which NoSQL type fits each piece?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Intended mapping: (1) document store for profiles, (2) column-family for the
GPS firehose, (3) graph for the referral relationships — the point is that one real system often
uses *multiple* NoSQL types for different parts of itself, not just one.
:::

---

## NoSQL vs. Relational — The Real Trade-off

| | Relational | NoSQL (general) |
|---|---|---|
| Schema | Fixed, enforced upfront | Flexible or absent |
| Joins | First-class, well-optimized | Limited or discouraged |
| Consistency | Strong, by default | Often tunable — your choice, per Session 2 |
| Horizontal scaling | Harder | Designed in from the start |
| Best for | Transactional, strongly related data | High-scale, flexible, or high-write-volume data |

::: {.callout-important}
Neither family is "better." The right choice depends on your data's shape, your consistency
needs, and your scale — the same design questions from Sessions 1–3, now pointed at a concrete
product decision instead of an abstract scenario.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 7 Q6 tests two of this table's rows directly (schema flexibility, and "no
universally superior option") — this slide is close to that question's own framing.
:::

## MongoDB Concepts

| MongoDB | Relational equivalent |
|---|---|
| Database | Database |
| Collection | Table |
| Document | Row |
| Field | Column |
| `_id` | Primary key (auto-generated) |

```python
from pymongo import MongoClient

client = MongoClient("mongodb+srv://...")
db     = client["my_database"]
col    = db["my_collection"]
```

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** This mapping table is worth reading straight through once — it's the
Rosetta Stone for everything that follows.
:::

---

## CRUD — Create

```python
# Insert one document
result = col.insert_one({
    "name": "Alice",
    "dept": "Engineering",
    "salary": 95000
})
print(result.inserted_id)  # the auto-generated _id

# Insert many documents at once
col.insert_many([
    {"name": "Bob",  "salary": 62000},
    {"name": "Carol","salary": 78000},
])
```

- `_id` is created automatically for every document — a unique identifier, unless you supply your
  own.
- `insert_one` returns one new `_id`; `insert_many` returns a list of them.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Quiz 7 Q8 tests `insertOne` syntax directly (shell form: `db.students.insertOne(...)`)
— note that the Python driver spells it `insert_one` (snake_case) while the MongoDB shell spells it
`insertOne` (camelCase); both are correct in their own context, and worth pointing out explicitly
since Lab 9 uses the Python form and Checkpoint 7 uses shell syntax.
:::

---

## CRUD — Read, and Query Operators

```python
# Find all documents
for doc in col.find():
    print(doc)

# Find with an exact-match filter
engineers = col.find({"dept": "Engineering"})

# Filter with a comparison operator
high_earners = col.find({"salary": {"$gt": 80000}})

# Sort and limit
col.find().sort("salary", -1).limit(5)   # top 5 by salary
```

| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `$gt` / `$lt` | Greater than / less than |
| `$gte` / `$lte` | ≥ / ≤ |
| `$ne` | Not equal |
| `$in` | Value is in a given list |
| `$exists` | Field exists on the document |

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Quiz 7 Q9 and Q10 both test this directly — `find({})` returns *everything*
(Q10), and `$lt` versus `$gt` (Q9). Say both of those out loud explicitly, they're easy to
mix up under quiz pressure.
:::

---

## CRUD — Update and Delete

```python
# Update ONE matching document
col.update_one(
    {"name": "Alice"},
    {"$set": {"salary": 100000}}
)

# Update ALL matching documents
col.update_many(
    {"dept": "Engineering"},
    {"$mul": {"salary": 1.10}}   # 10% raise for everyone matched
)

# Delete
col.delete_one({"name": "Bob"})
col.delete_many({"active": False})
```

- `$set` replaces a field's value outright; `$mul` multiplies a numeric field by a factor.
- `update_one`/`delete_one` affect only the **first** match; `update_many`/`delete_many` affect
  **every** match.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This maps almost exactly onto Checkpoint 7's Task 3 (updateOne + $set) and Task
4 (deleteMany) — don't use the checkpoint's own `active`/department fields as the live example
here if you want to avoid spoiling it outright, though the operators themselves obviously must be
taught plainly.
:::

---

## Replication in MongoDB

Session 1's general replication concept, applied concretely: MongoDB uses **replica sets** —
typically 3 nodes, 1 primary + 2 secondaries.

```
Write → Primary → Secondary 1
                → Secondary 2
Read ← Primary (default) or a Secondary (if read preference allows it)
```

- All writes go to the **primary**; changes replicate out to secondaries — asynchronously by
  default, which is Session 2's "eventual consistency" in a real product.
- If the primary fails, the remaining secondaries automatically elect a new primary.
- **Read preference** (Session 2's concept, by its real name here): `primary` (always current) or
  `secondaryPreferred` (may be slightly stale, spreads out read load).

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** This is the payoff moment for Session 1 and Session 2 — say explicitly "this is
the exact same replication and consistency material from last week, now with MongoDB's own
names on it."
:::

---

## Sharding in MongoDB

Session 1's general sharding concept, applied concretely: when a collection outgrows one machine,
split it across **shards** using a **shard key**.

```
Shard key: user_id

Shard 1: user_id 0 – 9,999,999
Shard 2: user_id 10,000,000 – 19,999,999
Shard 3: user_id 20,000,000+
```

- A router process (**`mongos`**) directs each query to the right shard(s), transparently to your
  application code — you don't write different queries for a sharded vs. unsharded collection.
- A poorly chosen shard key creates the **hot spots** Session 1 warned about — e.g., sharding by
  signup date sends all of today's traffic to one shard.
- In practice, each shard is *also* a replica set — sharding and replication are combined, not
  either/or, answering Session 1's "can a table need both?" callout question directly: yes.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Land the "combined, not either/or" point explicitly — it's the resolution to
the open question from Session 1's photo-sharing-app callout.
:::

## Beyond CRUD: Counting for the Capstone

One operation beyond plain CRUD is worth knowing now, because the capstone's `flask_app.py` needs
it for its dashboard's stat cards:

```python
# Count documents matching a filter
col.count_documents({"dept": "Engineering"})

# A simple aggregation: average salary
from pymongo import MongoClient
col.aggregate([
    {"$group": {"_id": None, "avg_salary": {"$avg": "$salary"}}}
])
```

- `count_documents(filter)` — how many documents match, without fetching them.
- MongoDB's full **aggregation pipeline** (multi-stage `$match`/`$group`/`$sort` chains) is more
  than this course goes deep on — the capstone only needs simple counts and averages like the
  example above, not the full pipeline syntax.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Keep this genuinely light — it exists so students aren't caught off guard by
`flask_app.py`'s stat-card queries, not to teach the aggregation pipeline as a topic in its own
right.
:::

---

## MongoDB Atlas — Cloud-Managed MongoDB

- No server to set up yourself — MongoDB Atlas hosts and manages it for you.
- Free tier (M0): enough storage for this course's work, no credit card required.
- Handles replication, backups, and monitoring automatically — the replica-set mechanics from two
  slides ago happen behind the scenes.
- Connection string format: `mongodb+srv://user:password@cluster.mongodb.net/`

::: {.callout-tip}
Atlas is what you'll use in Lab 9, the capstone, and — realistically — in most entry-level
industry jobs. The managed service is exactly what lets you use everything from today without
running a database server yourself.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** This is largely logistics for Friday's lab — keep it brief.
:::

## Module 5 Summary

| Concept | Key idea |
|---|---|
| Replication | Full copies of the data on multiple nodes — solves read throughput and availability |
| Sharding | Splitting the data itself across nodes — solves data volume and write throughput |
| Strong consistency | Every read reflects the latest write — costs write latency |
| Eventual consistency | Replicas converge over time — reads can briefly be stale |
| Document store | JSON-like documents, flexible schema — MongoDB |
| MongoDB CRUD | `insert_one/many`, `find`, `update_one/many`, `delete_one/many` |
| Replica set / sharded cluster | MongoDB's names for replication and sharding, combined in practice |

**Connects to:** Checkpoints 6 & 7, Quiz 7, Lab 9, Final Q31–Q45, Capstone (`spark_job.py`'s
direct-to-MongoDB writes, `flask_app.py`'s queries)
